items.title: Carter Benny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I think he also played something of Phil Woods’.

ctx.x: Just going a step further, you were once given a blindfold test by Leonard Feather, and he played you some Ornette Coleman, which was yet another development maybe beyond Coltrane on the continuum, I guess. Your reaction was not favorable at all. It was one of the strongest reactions I’ve seen in print from you. Was there nothing in that period or that type of music that you found, personally, anything worthwhile in?
On that particular blindfold test, I think he also played something of Phil Woods’.

items.title: 66095_Benny Carter oral history interview
items.q: Phil Woods on the other alto and Charlie Rouse on the other tenor, Coleman Hawkins, myself

ctx.x: Field, mentioned to me -- he'd like me to, you know, just use the saxophone section and recreate a couple of things that Coleman Hawkins and I had done in Paris many years earlier with the two French saxophone players, Andre Ekyan, the altoist, and Alex Combelle, who is a tenor saxophone player; so we got together, oh, Phil Woods on the other alto and Charlie Rouse on the other tenor, Coleman Hawkins, myself -- with Jimmy Garrison on base and Dick Katz on piano, and Joe Jones on drums and John Collins on guitar,…
And you did a few of the tunes of those famous brase.

items.title: Phil Woods — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: the first jazz I ever played were Benny Carter transcribed solos

ctx.x: I didn’t know. I had no idea. I thought you had to be anointed. I thought you had to learn to read music, I didn’t know that you could just start playing it, you know? So I went and started playing it, you know? He would give me the first lesson, the rumanic elementary, but uh I was just pleasing mom and uh ok great, and I put the horn back in the case and went about my business, put it back in the closet, and then I’d go for a lesson a week later and to make a long story short to say as they say, I could play the

lesson without even trying. You know, I didn’t think it was any big deal, and if I had gotten a teacher, one of those straight-laced cats, you know, who would say “Hey, you know, How dare you? You’re playing by ear.” You know, this is our best friend [points to his ear] this guy right here,” and then say ‘oops we have two of them.’ You know. And he recognized the fact that I must have a fair amount of retention, and I had a good sound, I always had a good tone. I mean I was built, that’s what I’m here for, that’s…

because Duke was always writing new music. So us kids, there were a bunch of us, in Springfield they used to call us the Springfield Rifles because uh well just briefly there was Hal Serra on piano who’s still around in New York, I just had lunch with him. Uh Sal Salvadore was on guitar, he later went with Stan Kenton. Joe Morello was our drummer who uh I think everybody knows who Joe Morello was but in case you were asleep he played with Dave Brubeck and did the first drum solo in “Take Five,” Paul Desmond’s…
